title: A light inside the globe
hook: Some map projections are literally shadows cast onto paper. Where does the far north land?

knows: that flat maps of the world exist in different projections
latitude in degrees north of the equator
doesNotKnow: that some projections are light through a globe onto paper
that the paper's shape decides what stretches

misconception: Projections are arbitrary redrawings, with no geometry behind them.
objective: The learner can explain that a projection is a rule for placing points on a surface, that a light at the centre with a cylinder at the equator puts latitude φ at tan φ radii (80°N at about 5.7), and that the stretch grows away from where the paper touches.

claims.text: With a light at the Earth's centre and a cylinder touching the equator, latitude φ lands tan φ globe radii above the equator: 80°N at 5.67 radii, 60°N at 1.73.
claims.source: Similar triangles in the cross-section: the ray through (cos φ, sin φ) meets x = 1 at y = tan φ. This is the central cylindrical projection, y = R tan φ (Snyder 1987, Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395; from memory, not checked online). tan 80° = 5.671, tan 60° = 1.732 (node). Demo.tsx landing() places the drawn ray with the same function. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: tan 80 = 5.671, tan 60 = 1.732; the ray through (cos p, sin p) from the centre meets x = 1 at y = tan p (central cylindrical projection).

claims.text: Measured along the globe's curve, 80°N is 1.40 radii from the equator.
claims.source: Arc length = angle in radians: 80 x π/180 = 1.396 radii. Shown as the green arc and the 'Along the globe' readout. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: 80 deg = 1.3963 rad = 1.40 radii of arc on a unit globe.

claims.text: With a flat sheet on the North Pole the stretch moves to the equator: latitude φ lands cot φ radii from the pole.
claims.source: Same cross-section: the ray meets y = 1 at x = cot φ (the gnomonic projection, polar aspect; Snyder 1987, from memory). 80°N lands at 0.18 radii; 10°N at 5.67; the equator never lands. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: cot 80 = 0.176 (0.18), cot 10 = 5.67; ray meets y = 1 at x = cot p (polar gnomonic); at the equator it is parallel to the sheet and never lands. Stage slider tops out at 80N and 0N reads 'never' for the sheet.

claims.text: With a light at the centre, paper that touches the globe along one line is true there and stretches everything away from it.
claims.source: For the cylinder, dy/dφ = sec² φ, which is 1 at the equator and grows without limit toward the pole; for the polar sheet the same holds measured from the pole. True of these two light projections; stated generally in the reveal as the idea of a tangent surface (Snyder 1987, ch. on developable surfaces; from memory). | Builder fix 2026-10-13 (pass 4): prefixed 'With a light at the centre,' per fact-check.

claims.text: A projection is a rule for putting each point of the globe on paper.
claims.source: Definition (Snyder 1987, ch. 1). The lesson does not claim that real atlases use the central cylindrical projection, nor that Mercator is a light projection (it is not). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Standard definition: a map projection is a systematic rule for transferring points of the globe to a plane (Snyder 1987, ch. 1). The reveal does not claim atlases use this projection.

recall.question: A light at the globe's centre shines onto a cylinder touching the equator. Which part of the map is stretched most?
recall.why: Latitude φ lands at tan φ radii, which grows without limit toward the poles; the paper is true only where it touches, at the equator.
